documents: The study utilizes a modified MedQA USMLE dataset where multiple-choice options are removed from the question stems to create free-response questions. The dataset includes only Step 2 and Step 3 USMLE questions that evaluate the task of diagnosing a patient.
A training set of 95 questions was used for iterative prompt development, and a test set of 518 questions was reserved for evaluation. The full test set is available in Supplementary Data 1.

The study evaluates the performance of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on open-ended clinical questions assessing diagnostic reasoning. GPT-4 performance is further evaluated on the diagnostically difficult NEJM case series.

The study compares traditional Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting with diagnostic reasoning prompts modeled after differential diagnosis formation, intuitive reasoning, analytical reasoning, and Bayesian inference.
Example LLM responses for each prompting strategy are located in Fig. 1 for GPT-3.5 and Fig. 2 for GPT-4, while full results are available in Supplementary Data 1 and 2.
The GPT-4 API generated an error for 20 questions of the test set, reducing the effective test set size to 498.
GPT-4 response and rationale results for the entire NEJM test set are included in Supplementary Data 2.
The study used a training set of 95 questions for iterative prompt development and reserved a test set of 518 questions for evaluation, with the full test set available in Supplementary Data 1.

GPT-4 performance was evaluated on the 310 most recently published cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) Case Records series, excluding 10 cases that lacked a definitive final diagnosis or exceeded the maximum context length of the GPT-4 API.
A full list of all included NEJM Case Records cases by title and DOI number is provided in Supplementary Data 2.

Five prompts were developed for the modified MedQA dataset: one traditional Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt and four clinical reasoning prompts (differential diagnosis, analytical, Bayesian, and intuitive reasoning), each including two example questions with rationales employing the target reasoning strategy.
The full prompts used for the MedQA dataset are provided in Table 2, and the full prompts used for the NEJM challenge set are provided in Supplementary Note 1.
The full text of the example questions is omitted for readability, and descriptive MedQA examples are located in Supplementary Data 4.
The study evaluated 100 GPT-4 diagnostic reasoning rationales to quantify the relationship between logical errors and incorrect answers.
The LLM response and rationale results for the entire test set are provided in Supplementary Information 1.
The analysis of logic errors in rationales is detailed in Supplementary Data 5.

The study's investigation was limited to the GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models, US-centric question sets, and the English language, which prevents generalization of the findings to other available models or non-English languages.
The authors developed diagnostic reasoning prompts using an iterative prompt engineering process and evaluated GPT-3.5 accuracy on the MEDQA training set, which is provided in Supplementary Data 3.
The experimental process involved experimenting with several different types of prompts, which are documented in Supplementary Note 2.

The study utilized the OpenAI Davinci-003 model via the OpenAI API to generate GPT-3.5 responses and the GPT-4 model via the OpenAI API to generate GPT-4 responses. The GPT-3.5 model was prompted using the Demonstrate-Search-Predict (DSP) method, while GPT-4 responses did not use DSP or self-consistency because those features were unavailable for GPT-4 at the time of submission.

Language model responses were evaluated by two blinded physicians from a panel of three internal medicine attending physicians and one internal medicine resident, with a third evaluator determining the final grade in cases of disagreement. Physicians used UpToDate, MKSAPP, and StatPearls to verify the accuracy of answers when needed.

Self-consistency was applied to all GPT-3.5 Chain-of-Thought prompts, and the computing was performed in a Google CoLab Jupyter Notebook. The full code for the evaluation is available in Supplementary Note 3, and the LLM response and rationale results for the entire test set are found in Supplementary Information 1.

Statistical analysis was performed in R using the epibasix library, and computing was performed in a Google CoLab Jupyter Notebook with full code available in Supplementary Note 3. Statistical significance was set at an alpha of 0.0125 to reflect multiple hypotheses (four prompts per each model) by the Bonferroni Correction.

Statistical significance and confidence intervals were calculated against traditional Chain of Thought using McNemar's test for paired proportions, two-tailed. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen's Kappa Statistic.
The first 100 GPT-4 differential diagnosis rationales were evaluated for appropriate logic and medical accuracy by physician authors RG and TS, who are both internal medicine attending physicians.

GPT-3.5 performance on a free-response MEDQA question set showed correct response percentages of 46% for Chain of Thought, 48% for Intuitive reasoning, 40% for Analytic reasoning, 38% for Differential diagnosis, and 42% for Bayesian inference. Percentage difference and p-value statistics were calculated compared to traditional chain-of-thought.

GPT-4 performance on a free-response MEDQA question set showed correct response percentages of 76% for Chain of Thought, 77% for Intuitive reasoning, 78% for Analytic reasoning, 78% for Differential diagnosis, and 72% for Bayesian inference. Percentage difference and p-value statistics were calculated compared to traditional chain-of-thought.

All data used in the manuscript, including all prompts, LLM responses, and reviewer grades, are provided in the Supplementary Information and open access figshare repository (10.6084/m9.figshare.24886593).
All code used in the manuscript is provided in the Supplementary Information and open access figshare repository (10.6084/m9.figshare.24886593).
The GPT-4 chain-of-thought prompt achieved 38% correct responses on the NEJM challenge question set, while the differential diagnosis prompt achieved 34% correct responses.
Reviewers were blinded to the index question, gold standard answer, and grade of the LLM response when identifying instances of inaccuracy or false logic in diagnostic reasoning rationales.

The inter-rater agreement for the GPT-4 NEJM evaluation was 97% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.93, and the GPT-4 response and rationale results for the entire NEJM test set are included in Supplementary Data 2.

The exact text for the Traditional Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt is: "Provide a step-by-step deduction that identifies the correct response {Example Question 1} Example Rationale 1: The patient had a surgical repair of a displaced femoral neck fracture. The patient has petechiae. The patient has a new oxygen requirement, meaning they are having difficulty with their breathing. This patient most likely has a fat embolism. {Example Question 2} Example Rationale 2: This patient is having chest pain. They recently had a heart attack and has new chest pain, suggesting he may have a problem with his heart. The EKG has diffuse ST elevations and he has a scratching murmur. This patient likely has Dressler Syndrome."

The exact text for the Differential Diagnosis CoT prompt is: "Use step by step deduction to create a differential diagnosis and then use step by step deduction to determine the correct response. {Example Question 1} Example Rationale 1: This patient has shortness of breath after a long bone surgery. The differential for this patient is pulmonary embolism, fat embolism, myocardial infarction, blood loss, anaphylaxis, or a drug reaction. The patient has petechiae which makes fat embolism more likely. This patient most likely has a fat embolism. {Example Question 2} Example Rationale 2: This patient has chest pain with diffuse ST elevations after a recent myocardial infarction. The differential for this patient includes: myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, pericarditis, Dressler syndrome, aortic dissection, and costochondritis. This patient likely has a high-pitched scratching sound on auscultation associated with pericarditis and Dressler Syndrome. This patient has diffuse ST elevations associated with Dressler Syndrome. This patient most likely has Dressler Syndrome."

The exact text for the Intuitive Reasoning CoT prompt is: "Use symptom, signs, and laboratory disease associations to step by step deduce the correct response. {Example Question 1} Example Rationale 1: This patient has findings of petechiae, altered mental status, shortness of breath, and recent surgery suggesting a diagnosis of fat emboli. The patient most likely has a fat embolism. {Example Question 2} Example Rationale 2: This patient had a recent myocardial infarction with new development of diffuse ST elevations, chest pain, and a high pitched scratching murmur which are found in Dressler's syndrome. This patient likely has Dressler's Syndrome."

The exact text for the Analytic Reasoning CoT prompt is: "Use analytic reasoning to deduce the physiologic or biochemical pathophysiology of the patient and step by step identify the correct response. {Example Question 1} Example Rationale 1: The patient recently had large bone surgery making fat emboli a potential cause because the bone marrow was manipulated. Petechiae can form in response to capillary inflammation caused by fat emboli. Fat micro globules cause CNS microcirculation occlusion causing confusion and altered mental status. Fat obstruction in the pulmonary arteries can cause tachycardia and shortness of breath as seen in this patient. This patient most likely has a fat embolism. {Example Question 2} Example Rationale 2: This patient had a recent myocardial infarction which can cause myocardial inflammation that causes pericarditis and Dressler Syndrome. The diffuse ST elevations and high pitched scratching murmur can be signs of pericardial inflammation as the inflamed pericardium rubs against the pleura as seen with Dressler Syndrome. This patient likely has Dressler Syndrome."

The exact text for the Bayesian Reasoning CoT prompt is: "Use step-by-step Bayesian Inference to create a prior probability that is updated with new information in the history to produce a posterior probability and determine the final diagnosis. {Example Question 1} Example Rationale 1: The prior probability of fat embolism is 0.05% however the patient has petechiae on exam which is seen with fat emboli, which increases the posterior probability of fat embolism to 5%. Altered mental status increases the probability further to 10%. Recent orthopedic surgery increases the probability of fat emboli syndrome to 60%. This patient most likely has a fat embolism. {Example Question 2} Example Rationale 2: The prior probability of Dressler Syndrome is 0.01%. The patient has diffuse ST elevations, increasing the probability of Dressler Syndrome to 5%. The patient has a scratching murmur which increases the probability to 10%. In the setting of a recent MI the posterior probability of myocardial infarction is 55%. This patient likely has Dressler Syndrome."
The DSP (Demonstrate-Search-Predict) framework code is available at the GitHub repository stanfordnlp/dspy, specifically at version v1 (https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/tree/v1).
The OpenAI GPT-3.5 API (text-davinci-003) and GPT-4 API were accessed via the platform at https://platform.openai.com in 2023.
The supplementary material for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-024-01010-1, and correspondence regarding materials should be addressed to Thomas Savage.

The study benchmarks multiple large language model versions and a retrieval-augmented generation workflow on a curated dataset of 2000 medical cases derived from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care database.
The study utilizes a dataset of 2000 real-world cases from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) database to evaluate model performance.
The evaluation benchmarks multiple versions of the Claude family of large language models and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agentic workflow.

The specific clinical care aspects predicted by the LLM workflows are triage level (Emergency Severity Index), patient referral to medical specialty, and diagnosis based on symptoms, patient information, and initial vitals.

The study used a curated dataset derived from the fully de-identified MIMIC-IV ED dataset and MIMIC-IV Notes, extracting 2000 medical cases to simulate emergency department clinical decision-making. The dataset is not directly publicly available, which prevents contamination from LLM training data.

The model evaluation tested three specific versions from the Claude family: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Claude 3 Haiku. Additionally, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system was developed to assist Claude 3.5 Sonnet using a knowledge base of 30 million PubMed abstracts.
The study results are presented in Figure 3 and Table 1, with confusion matrices for the two best-performing models in each accuracy evaluation displayed in Figure 4.

Table 2 presents the performance comparison between general user and clinical user models, showing a performance increase in triage level prediction across all models when provided with more detailed information.
The study utilized the MIMIC-IV dataset, which prohibits the use of external APIs like OpenAI's GPT-4 due to privacy regulations, necessitating the use of AWS Privatelink to connect to Claude models.

The system architecture differentiates between two user types: general users who provide only personal information and symptoms (history of present illness), and clinicians who can additionally retrieve initial clinical data including temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure.
The RAG workflow used in the paper relies on a knowledge base of 30 million PubMed abstracts to improve output with domain-specific context.

The study evaluates LLM performance on the MIMIC-IV-ED dataset using the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), which classifies patients into five levels ranging from ESI 1 (immediate life-saving interventions) to ESI 5 (treatment can be safely delayed).

The evaluation assesses LLM triage prediction capabilities for two specific user scenarios: a general user providing only symptom-based information and a clinician with access to initial clinical data.

Model results are assessed using exact match accuracy, where the predicted triage level must match the actual value, and triage range accuracy, where predictions are correct if they are exactly or one triage level higher than the actual level, with the exception that triage level 1 must be predicted as 1.

The results for the LLM diagnosis prediction evaluation are presented in Figure 6 and Table 1, which display the accuracy percentages for two evaluation methods: matched diagnosis and at least one diagnosis match.
Table 2 presents the specific performance data showing improvements in the clinical user model over the general user model for the RAG-assisted LLM.
Figure 6 displays the diagnosis prediction accuracy percentages for both the matched diagnosis and at least one diagnosis match evaluation methods across different LLMs.

The MIMIC-IV-ED and MIMIC-IV-Notes datasets lack exact information on the medical specialist for referral, so Claude 3.5 Sonnet was used to create a ground truth by predicting the most likely specialist for each patient diagnosis.
The ground truth generation process and the specific prompt used to predict specialties with Claude 3.5 Sonnet are detailed in the "Methods: Prompts" section.
Four clinicians reviewed a subset of the LLM-generated ground truth to validate whether the assigned specialties appropriately matched the corresponding diagnoses.
The LLMs were evaluated in two scenarios, general user and clinical user models, where each model was asked to predict the top three specialties for handling patient cases.

Table 1 reports exact performance metrics for RAG-Assisted LLM, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Claude 3 Haiku across triage level, specialty, and diagnosis tasks using exact match, range, and at least one evaluation methods.

The evaluation of predicted diagnoses against ground truth diagnoses used the model Claude 3.5 Sonnet as the judge. The validation of this LLM-as-judge approach involved four clinicians reviewing a subset of the data to compare predicted diagnoses to ground truth diagnoses.

Figure 4 presents confusion matrices for triage level prediction for the models RAG-Assisted Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The matrices cover General User and Clinical User settings and use exact match and range evaluation methods.

Table 2 reports performance improvement for RAG-Assisted LLM, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Claude 3 Haiku from general user to clinical user settings. The metrics include Triage Level (Exact Match, Range), Specialty (Matched, At Least One), and Diagnosis (Matched, At Least One).

The study evaluated inter-rater agreement between two specific LLMs, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and a RAG-assisted LLM, and four clinicians regarding predicted diagnoses versus ground truth. The clinicians categorized predictions into four levels: Exact Match, Clinically Equivalent, Clinically Related, or Incorrect, while the LLMs provided a binary evaluation of whether the prediction exactly matched or fell within a broader related category.

Clinician 2 exhibited a higher error rate of 9.15% compared to the average error rate of 0.68% for the other clinicians, indicating stricter evaluation standards. Confusion matrices for the two clinician pairs are provided in Supplementary Fig. 8 and 9 to illustrate these variations in human evaluation.

Table 3 reports the average inter-model agreement percentages for triage level and specialty predictions among the RAG-Assisted LLM, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Claude 3 Haiku, with specific values such as 85.94% between the General and Clinical User for the RAG-Assisted LLM.

Table 4 presents the clinician validation results for LLM-generated specialties, showing that Clinician 1 recorded 93.77% accuracy and 0% error rate, while the overall average across all clinicians was 81.5% accuracy and 2.63% error rate.
The inter-model agreement analysis for diagnosis data was omitted because the data has the highest variability and requires assessment by an LLM judge.
Full results for inter-model agreement across the triage and specialty datasets are available in Supplementary Table 2.
The RAG-Assisted LLM demonstrated the highest average agreement across all models, closely followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
The highest single inter-model agreement was between Claude 3.5 Sonnet and the RAG-assisted LLM.
Four clinicians independently reviewed a subset of the dataset to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the LLM-generated specialties.
Clinicians categorized each LLM-generated specialty as Correct, Partially Correct, Reasonable but Suboptimal, or Incorrect.
Two clinicians reviewed the same subset of the dataset to provide an independent evaluation and objectivity.
The study utilizes the Claude 3.5 Sonnet model and a RAG-assisted version of Claude 3.5 Sonnet to evaluate clinical decision-making tasks.
The RAG-assisted LLM and base Claude 3.5 Sonnet model were evaluated using a clinical user setting that includes additional patient vitals data.
The RAG workflow incorporates external sources from a research context to provide informed perspectives on input data.

The RAG-assisted LLM demonstrates strong performance in exact accuracy on triage level data with vital signs information, but this does not necessarily improve range accuracy for predicting severity levels.

The LLM binary output "True" was mapped to clinician ratings of "Exact Match" or "Clinically Equivalent", while "False" was mapped to "Clinically Related" or "Incorrect". Each diagnostic subset was reviewed by two clinicians to evaluate agreement under Union and Intersection conditions.

In the Union scenario, an LLM evaluation was considered correct if at least one of the two clinicians agreed with the LLM's rating. In the Intersection scenario, an LLM evaluation was considered correct only if both clinicians agreed with the LLM's rating.

Under the Union scenario, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an accuracy of 95.62% and the RAG-assisted LLM achieved an accuracy of 94.91%. Under the Intersection scenario, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an accuracy of 70.74% and the RAG-assisted LLM achieved an accuracy of 69.86%.
The study benchmarked Large Language Models on 2000 real-world medical cases sourced from the MIMIC-IV-ED dataset to predict diagnoses, recommend specialists, and determine care urgency.

Table 5 reports specific Inter-Rater Accuracy percentages for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and the RAG-assisted LLM, with individual clinician values ranging from 76.51% to 90.43% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 77.78% to 90.11% for the RAG-assisted LLM.

The average Inter-Rater Union Accuracy was 95.62% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 94.91% for the RAG-assisted LLM, while the average Inter-Rater Intersection Accuracy was 70.74% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 69.86% for the RAG-assisted LLM.
Confusion matrices for the evaluation results between the two clinician pairs are provided in Supplementary Fig. 10 and 11.

The study focused on Claude models, and the specific model versions mentioned for potential future evaluation include OpenAI models with the "Deep Research" function and Claude 3.7 Sonnet with its "extended thinking mode".
The study extracted the History of Present Illness (HPI) from clinical notes to limit bias, as real-time audio or video recordings of initial patient contact were unavailable.
The specific LLM versions tested included Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Claude 3.5.
The study utilized a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow to provide external sources to the Large Language Models (LLMs).
The study experimented with various prompts to guide the LLMs, noting that task framing significantly impacts result quality.
The researchers set the temperature parameter to zero to ensure consistent and reliable outputs, observing identical results across runs.
The researchers decided to run the LLM predictions only once for the final evaluation due to cost constraints and to mimic a clinical environment where a clinician relies on the first output.
The specific prompts used to guide the LLM in performing clinical tasks are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1-6.
The data preprocessing pipeline utilized MIMIC-IV-ED 2.2 and MIMIC-IV-Note from Physionet, merging necessary data tables before processing and cleaning.
The study employed AWS Privatelink to securely connect to Claude models hosted on AWS to comply with privacy regulations restricting the use of the MIMIC-IV dataset with external APIs.
The curated dataset was constructed using the MIMIC-IV ED dataset and the MIMIC-IV Notes dataset.
Triage information was obtained from the MIMIC-IV-ED 'triage' file, while patient demographics such as race and gender were extracted from the 'edstays' file.
Patient age was specifically extracted from the MIMIC-IV 'patients' file.
Initial vital signs were extracted from the MIMIC-IV-ED 'triage' file, and unstructured clinical notes were extracted from the MIMIC-IV-Note 'discharge' file.
The clinical user input required initial vital signs including temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure.

The dataset was constructed by merging MIMIC-IV "patients" demographics, MIMIC-IV-ED "triage" vital signs, and MIMIC-IV-Note "discharge" notes, linked via the MIMIC-IV-ED "edstays" file using the stay_id identifier.

Data preprocessing required filtering records to retain only those with sequence number (seq_num) equal to 1 to ensure unique emergency department stays, dropping duplicate subject entries, removing cases with missing triage information, and excluding patients that had died.

Unstructured clinical notes were preprocessed by extracting only the history of present illness paragraph, discarding other note information, and selecting cases with history of present illness string lengths between 50 and 2000 characters.
The preprocessing pipeline removed clinical note entries that mentioned "ED" or "ER" to exclude references lacking necessary patient symptom information.
Diagnosis extraction used only primary diagnoses from clinical notes and discarded cases containing more than 15 primary diagnoses.
The study implements a RAG-assisted LLM framework using Claude 3.5 Sonnet as the language model component and incorporates a multistep process for query processing and answer generation.
The triage level evaluation framework is based on the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), which consists of five levels outlined in Supplementary Table 1.

The triage range evaluation framework allows model predictions to be one level more severe than the ground truth (e.g., a real value of 3 allows predictions of 2 or 3), except for a real value of 1 which requires a prediction of 1.

The specialty evaluation framework assesses LLM performance by generating top three specialty recommendations based on patient information, distinguishing between general user inputs (symptoms and basic information) and clinical user inputs (augmented with initial vital signs).
The RAG system utilizes Sonnet as the Large Language Model component and relies on a knowledge base consisting of 30 million PubMed abstracts converted into embedding vectors.

The workflow begins with query decomposition, breaking patient queries into smaller components that are embedded and compared via semantic similarity to the vector database of 30 million PubMed abstracts to retrieve relevant information.

The Sonnet LLM generates responses supported by the retrieved data and provides source PubMed references, followed by an iterative critique-refinement loop where the LLM evaluates outputs for gaps or inaccuracies to enhance performance.

The study used Claude 3.5 Sonnet to predict the most likely medical specialist for each diagnosis in MIMIC-IV-ED and MIMIC-IV-Notes cases to establish ground truth, as the datasets lack exact information on which specialist each patient visited.
The evaluation protocol requires predicting the top three specialists for each case to align with the multi-specialty ground truth and avoid bias toward a single diagnosis.

The diagnosis evaluation framework predicts a top three list of diagnoses for each case and compares these predictions to actual diagnoses, restricting the dataset to patients with a hospital stay duration of less than one day to exclude diagnoses arising later in hospitalization.

A subset of the dataset was validated by four clinicians from Policlinico Gemelli in Rome, Italy, the Radiology Department at Klinikum rechts der Isar in Munich, Germany, and the University of Chicago in the United States.
The LLM evaluator compared each of the top three predicted diagnoses directly to the ground truth to determine whether they aligned in meaning or category.

The LLM judge was provided the true list of diagnoses for each patient and three predicted diagnoses, and was instructed to determine if a predicted diagnosis matched a primary diagnosis via semantic equivalence or if it fell under a broader category related to the real diagnosis.
The LLM judge returned "True" if the predicted diagnosis matched the real one or was related to it in a broader sense, and returned "False" otherwise.
The prompt used for the LLM evaluation is located in the Methods: Prompts section of the document.
The evaluation of predicted diagnoses used an LLM judge to determine if a predicted diagnosis matched the ground truth or fit into a broader category of an actual diagnosis.
A subset of the dataset was reviewed by four clinicians who compared predicted diagnoses to ground truth diagnoses, with details located in the subsection "Reader Study".

The first specialty evaluation method calculated a score by dividing the count of correctly predicted specialties by the length of the shorter list between the ground truth and prediction lists for each patient.
The overall accuracy for the first specialty evaluation method was calculated by summing the points across all patients and dividing by the total number of patients.
The second specialty evaluation framework considered a patient's prediction successful if at least one of the model's predicted specialties appeared in the ground truth list.

The study used a subset of 400 cases out of 2000 from the dataset, with Clinicians 1 and 2 reviewing the same 200 cases and Clinicians 3 and 4 reviewing a different 200 cases to allow for independent evaluations.
Clinicians evaluated the LLM-generated ground truth specialty for each diagnosis by categorizing predictions into four levels: Correct, Partially Correct, Reasonable but Suboptimal, and Incorrect.

For the second task, clinicians compared the predicted diagnoses from the clinical user setting of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and the RAG-assisted LLM against ground truth diagnoses, categorizing results as Exact Match, Clinically Equivalent, Clinically Related, or Incorrect.
Core data is available at https://physionet.org/content/mimic-iv-note/2.2/ and data processing scripts with processed data are available at https://github.com/BIMSBbioinfo/medLLMbenchmark.
The code to process data is available at https://github.com/BIMSBbioinfo/medLLMbenchmark.

The intra-model agreement evaluation compared predictions from eight model variants, consisting of the RAG-assisted model and three Claude language models with general user and clinical user settings.
The MIMIC-IV dataset is available at PhysioNet via https://doi.org/10.13026/HXP0-HG59.
The MIMIC-IV-ED dataset is available at PhysioNet via https://doi.org/10.13026/5NTK-KM72.
The MIMIC-IV-Note dataset of deidentified free-text clinical notes is available at PhysioNet via https://doi.org/10.13026/1N74-NE17.
The study utilized the Claude 3.5 Sonnet model, documented at https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-5-sonnet.
Supplementary material for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-025-01684-1.

The study did not report the exact temperature or top-k sampling parameters used during inference on the modified MedQA and NEJM datasets, preventing verification of whether results were driven by prompt engineering or stochastic variance.

The reported 1.7% difference in intuitive reasoning performance has a 95% confidence interval ranging from -2.5% to 5.9%, which includes zero and prevents establishing directionality for replication purposes.

The specific multiple-comparison corrections applied to the five prompt variants are not provided, leaving the Type I error rate inflated and the statistical validity of the significant findings unreplicable.

Replication is blocked because the study does not report the exact multiple-comparison adjustment method or a proper power analysis for the five prompt variants, making it impossible to quantify the reliability of the observed consistency against the high variance of the 46% baseline accuracy.

The absence of reported random seeds and specific pipeline details constitutes a critical gap that prevents verification of whether the model's output is derived from genuine logical deduction or merely pattern-matching plausible medical text to satisfy the prompt structure.

A critical reproducibility gap exists because the study lacks a standardized preprocessing pipeline for the NEJM clinical vignettes, specifically missing normalization for length and complexity, which prevents the isolation of model reasoning limits from input distribution variance.

The evaluation is blocked by the absence of raw logs and reproducibility data, which are required to determine if the observed interpretability is a stable model feature or a fragile artifact of the specific, unreproducible experimental setup.

The DT-GPT model leverages electronic health records for clinical trajectory prediction without requiring data imputation or normalization. DT-GPT was benchmarked on non-small cell lung cancer, intensive care unit, and Alzheimer's disease datasets.
Generative AI methods for predicting patient trajectories include recurrent neural networks, transformers, and stable diffusion.
Causal machine learning algorithms face limitations related to small datasets or being confined to simulations.
Most foundation models for patient forecasting focus on single-point predictions rather than comprehensive longitudinal patient trajectories.
Clinically focused, LLM-inspired methods evaluate single-point predictions rather than longitudinal trajectories and do not use the knowledge of pretrained LLMs.

The LLM-based DT-GPT framework performs zero-shot forecasting on clinical variables not used during training and generates longitudinal forecasts for specific variables such as neutrophil and hemoglobin blood levels. The system also identifies key variables and responds to inquiries about them.

Existing LLM-based forecasting methods like LSTPrompt, LLMTime, Time-LLM, and GPT4TS utilize channel independence, which processes multivariate time series separately without modeling inter-series dependencies. This assumption is suboptimal for clinical trajectory forecasting where time series are correlated by causal biological links.

The proposed digital twins leverage data from electronic health records (EHRs) containing patient demographics, diagnoses, and lab results over time. EHRs present specific challenges for machine learning, including data heterogeneity, rare events, sparsity, and quality issues.

The DT-GPT model is based on finetuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on clinical data using a straightforward data encoding scheme and is designed to be model-agnostic without requiring architectural changes to any text-focused LLM.

The DT-GPT model was evaluated on three specific datasets: the MIMIC-IV dataset containing 35,131 Intensive Care Unit patients for short-term forecasting, the Flatiron Health EHR-derived de-identified database containing 16,496 non-small cell lung cancer patients for medium-term forecasting, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset containing 1,140 patients for long-term forecasting.

Specific details regarding task setup, data preprocessing, model training, and evaluation for the DT-GPT model are provided in the "Methods" section and Supplementary Tables 1-5 and Supplementary Note 1.

DT-GPT is a fine-tuned 7-billion-parameter model based on BioMistral, while Qwen3 is a 32-billion-parameter model. The benchmark includes 14 baselines: Linear Regression, LightGBM, Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Transformer, Time-series Dense Encoder (TiDE), Time-LLM, LLMTime, and PatchTST.

The NSCLC task predicts six laboratory values (Hemoglobin, Leukocytes, Lymphocytes/Leukocytes, Lymphocytes, Neutrophils, Lactate Dehydrogenase) weekly for up to 13 weeks post-therapy using pretreatment data. The ICU task forecasts respiratory rate, magnesium, and oxygen saturation for the next 24 hours based on the previous 24-hour history.

The Alzheimer's task forecasts Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes (CDR-SB), and Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS11) scores over the next 24 months at 6-month intervals using baseline measurements. All model comparisons were performed on unseen patients.

The evaluation metric is the scaled mean absolute error (MAE) using z-score scaling to allow comparison across variables. The benchmark results are presented in Table 1, showing scaled MAE for each model across the NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's datasets.

DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.55 ± 0.04 on the NSCLC dataset, 0.59 ± 0.03 on the ICU dataset, and 0.47 ± 0.03 on the Alzheimer's disease dataset. The second-best models were LightGBM with 0.57 ± 0.05 on NSCLC, LightGBM with 0.60 ± 0.03 on ICU, and Temporal Fusion Transformer with 0.48 ± 0.02 on Alzheimer's disease.

Statistical significance for DT-GPT over the second-best model was reported with a p-value < 9.6162 × 10^-17 for the NSCLC dataset and a p-value < 0.00043 for the ICU dataset, with details in Supplementary Note 2, Supplementary Tables 18-19, and Supplementary Figs. 1-2.

DT-GPT outperformed Bio-Mistral by 47.9% on NSCLC, 29.1% on ICU, and 61.1% on Alzheimer's disease, and outperformed the Qwen3-32B model by 22.9% on NSCLC, 19.9% on ICU, and 21.1% on Alzheimer's disease.
The absolute MAE values for DT-GPT are provided in Supplementary Tables 6-17.

DT-GPT forecasting performance was evaluated using scaled MAE, absolute MAE, mean absolute scaled error (MASE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE), and Spearman Correlation, while classification performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for clinically low/high predictions and overall trends.

DT-GPT achieved a ROC AUC of 0.506 for forecasting critically low hemoglobin levels (<7.5 g/dL) and a ROC AUC of 0.578 for predicting high leukocyte counts (>11.0 x 10^9/L), which was lower than the copy-forward baseline ROC AUC of 0.616.

DT-GPT achieved a ROC AUC of 0.793 for detecting mild anemia (hemoglobin below reference) and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (>222 U/L), and captured three-week trends in hemoglobin with ROC AUCs of 0.704 for increasing and 0.638 for decreasing.
The final prediction for DT-GPT is derived by averaging 30 generated trajectories.
Selecting individual trajectories with the lowest scaled MAE on the NSCLC dataset achieves a 26% improvement in error to 0.40 ± 0.02 without further model training.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic was computed across all target variables in the NSCLC cohort to compare predicted and true distributions.

DT-GPT performance degradation occurred only after more than 20% of the input was randomly masked, on top of the 94.4% initial missingness of the NSCLC dataset. DT-GPT was stable to misspellings in the input, only significantly degrading in performance after 25 misspellings per patient sample.

Explanatory variables were extracted from 25,575 out of 27,730 chatbot responses for the DT-GPT model. The most influential variables identified for the predictions were therapy, ECOG status, and leukocyte count.

Supplementary Table 22 contains scaled MAE values for DT-GPT and the LightGBM baseline. Supplementary Fig. 10 and Supplementary Table 23 provide data on zero-shot predictions and feature importance analysis for variables like the ferritin-to-hemoglobin ratio and Albumin-Bilirubin (ALBI) score components.

Fig. 3 presents histograms and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance metrics comparing the distribution of DT-GPT forecasted values against ground truth data. Fig. 4 displays mean absolute error (MAE) results assessing DT-GPT's robustness to varying patient counts, added missingness on top of a baseline 94.4% missingness in the NSCLC dataset, and injected misspellings.
The study extracted 81,004 trajectories from 81,918 forecasting results for 69 non-target clinical variables to evaluate DT-GPT's zero-shot performance.
The benchmark comparison used 69 LightGBM models, each trained on data from over 13,000 patients for individual target variables, against a single DT-GPT model in a zero-shot setting.
Specific LOINC codes for related variables are segmented neutrophils (30451-9), band form neutrophils (26507-4), neutrophils by automated count (751-8), and the target variable neutrophils (26499-4).
Scaled MAE values for DT-GPT and the LightGBM baseline are provided in Supplementary Table 22.
The NSCLC dataset has a baseline missingness of 94.4%, and the evaluation assesses the impact of added missingness and injected misspellings on the Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
The abbreviation 'Lymph./Leuk.' refers to lymphocytes/leukocytes in the data.

Fine-tuning is necessary for optimal performance, as non-fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) show lower accuracy than fine-tuned models even when the non-fine-tuned models are significantly larger.
The DT-GPT model's generative nature allows for multiple trajectory simulations per patient to provide insights into patient scenarios, cohort simulations, and uncertainty estimates.
DT-GPT operates without data normalization or imputation requirements and handles mixed data encodings, such as varying drug dosage formats, without additional preprocessing.

The evaluation of DT-GPT's zero-shot forecasting capability involved training 69 separate LightGBM models on other variables to compare against the single DT-GPT model, which received no further training.
In the comparison between DT-GPT and the 69 LightGBM models, DT-GPT outperformed the LightGBM models on 13 out of 69 non-target variables.
Figure 5b presents the five most important variables for predicting all variables derived from forecasting test patient samples, with each sample having 10 predicted trajectories.

The BioMistral 7B model was trained on a vast amount of biomedical databases and publications, which serves as a potential confounding factor for the interpretability hypotheses regarding latent clinical knowledge.
The current constraint on the number of forecasted variables in the DT-GPT model is due to the limited sequence length of the input and output of the LLMs used in fine-tuning.
Modeling of additional patient variables requires advances in extending context length, such as by using larger, more advanced models like Qwen3-32B as the base model.
Transitioning from zero-shot to few-shot learning, where the model receives further training on a small subset of data, is anticipated to enable a wider span of forecasted variables.

The DT-GPT method employs pre-trained large language models fine-tuned on clinical data and is agnostic regarding the underlying large language model architecture, allowing application to any general-purpose or specialized text-focused large language model without architectural changes.

DT-GPT was trained and evaluated for forecasting patients' laboratory values across three independent datasets: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), intensive care unit (ICU), and Alzheimer's disease patients.

The US-based non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) dataset used the nationwide Flatiron Health EHR-derived de-identified database, which comprises de-identified patient-level structured and unstructured data curated via technology-enabled abstraction.
During the study period, the de-identified data in the Flatiron Health database originated from approximately 280 cancer clinics, representing roughly 800 sites of care.
DT-GPT's applicability to broader clinical challenges would be extended by -shot learning, where the model receives further training on a small subset of data.
Forecasting performance for DT-GPT can be improved by adapting patching and prompt-as-aprefix from Time-LLM and normalization and generation of continuous likelihoods from LLMTime for clinical use.

DT-GPT exhibits a tendency to hallucinate, which is reflected in explainability results not necessarily providing true answers, requiring a human-in-the-loop setup and advanced training of clinicians on the use of LLM outputs.

DT-GPT recreates biases from the underlying data, which is especially pronounced in minority populations, necessitating methodological work, training of users, and the gathering of large scale, diverse clinical datasets.

High error predictions in DT-GPT occur due to high variance between multiple generated trajectories of each patient sample, where the mean aggregation into the final prediction does not capture key dynamics.

An open challenge for DT-GPT is to develop improved aggregation methods for generated trajectories, for example by using a second LLM as an arbiter or by having a human expert select the most realistic trajectory.

The deidentified NSCLC data originated from approximately 280 cancer clinics (~800 sites of care) and included 16,496 patients diagnosed between 01 January 1991 and 06 July 2023. Patients with a birth year of 1938 or earlier may have an adjusted birth year in the Flatiron Health datasets due to de-identification requirements.

The study data was harmonized by aggregating all values in a week based on the last observed value and focused on the 50 most common diagnoses and 80 most common laboratory measurements, resulting in 773,607 patient-days across 320 variables.

For every NSCLC patient, the trajectory was divided into input and output segments based on the start date of each line of therapy, with all variables up to the start date considered input data. The prediction objective was to predict weekly values up to 13 weeks after the start date for hemoglobin (718-7), leukocytes (26464-8), lymphocytes/leukocytes (26478-8), lymphocytes (26474-7), neutrophils (26499-4), and lactate dehydrogenase (2532-0).

The ICU analysis utilized the publicly-accessible Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) dataset and employed an established processing pipeline, resulting in 300 input variables across 1,686,288 time points from 35,131 patients.
The MIMIC-IV dataset processing pipeline generated 300 input variables across 1,686,288 time points from 35,131 patients to predict future hourly lab variables given the first 24 hours in the ICU.

The MIMIC-IV forecasting task specifically targets the next 24 hourly values for O2 saturation pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, and magnesium, which were selected for having the highest temporal variability and at least 50% patient measurement coverage.
The Alzheimer's disease dataset used for generalizability testing is based on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database available at adni.loni.usc.edu.

The ADNI dataset preprocessing included 1140 patients, with the task defined as predicting the 24-month trajectory of Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes (CDR-SB), and Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS11) given baseline measurements.

The study utilized the open-source biomedical LLM BioMistral 7B DARE, which was fine-tuned using standard cross-entropy loss masked to compute gradients only on output text. All hyperparameters for the DT-GPT fine-tuning process are documented in Supplementary Note 5.
During evaluation, the model performed 30 predictions for each patient sample, and the mean of these predictions was taken for each time point to determine the final output.
The missing data study involved randomly masking between 0 and 80% of data in addition to existing missing values, evaluated on a randomly sampled subset of 200 patients from the test set.

The noise study applied a misspelling algorithm that randomly performed perturbation, insertion, deletion, or replacement operations using all ASCII letters and digits across the entire input text, including dates, variable names, values, baseline information, and prompts.

The NSCLC and ICU datasets were split at the patient level into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test sets, with the ICU dataset split randomly and the NSCLC dataset stratified by group stage, smoking status, number of observations per visit, and number of visits with drug administrations.
The Alzheimer's disease dataset was randomly split into 80% training and 20% test sets due to small sample size, with hyperparameters determined via a further splitting on the training set.

A two-step outlier filtering procedure was applied to all datasets where target values below or above three standard deviations were first filtered out, followed by clipping target values to new standard deviation values calculated on the filtered dataset.
Data for all baselines excluding DT-GPT were standardized using z-scores.

Patient trajectories were encoded using manually developed templates for input and JSON-format encoding for output, structured into four components: patient history, demographic data, forecast dates, and prompt.
The study randomly sampled 200 patients from the test set to evaluate the DT-GPT model, a choice that increases result variance but allows for more extensive exploration.

The DT-GPT model was used for a chatbot and zero-shot learning tasks by first generating forecasting results from patient history and then adding a task-specific prompt surrounded by instruction-indication tokens to the chat history.
Example prompts and chatbot interactions for prediction explanation and zero-shot forecasting are provided in Supplementary Note 7 and Fig. 5a, e.

The forecasting metrics used to quantify predictive accuracy are mean absolute error (MAE), scaled MAE, mean absolute scaled error (MASE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE), and Spearman correlation coefficient.
The scaled MAE is calculated by dividing the MAE by the standard deviation of the clinical variable after outlier filtering.
The MASE is calculated by dividing the MAE by the mean absolute difference between observed values and baseline values across all subjects and time steps.
The SMAPE calculation includes an indicator function to avoid division by zero when the sum of the absolute values of the observed and predicted clinical variables is zero.

The weighted AUC ROC metric is calculated by weighting the individual AUC values for 'low', 'normal', and 'high' classes by the count of observed variable values in each respective class, as defined in Equation (6).

A predicted variable value is classified as a 'decreasing trend' only if the value decreases at every consecutive time step within the preceding lookback window of length s, and as an 'increasing trend' only if it increases at every consecutive time step within that same interval.

Forecasted values are excluded from the trend analysis if the time since the last input measurement is less than the lookback window length s to ensure a complete lookback window is available for classification.

The scaled MAE metric is defined as the sum of absolute differences between actual and predicted values divided by the sum of the absolute values of the actual and predicted values, using an indicator function to avoid division by zero.

The Spearman correlation coefficient is calculated using a rank function that orders values from lowest to highest, assigning the average rank to data points with identical values, and normalizing by the mean ranks of actual and predicted values.
The scaled MAE metric is designated as the primary evaluation metric because it permits comparison across all variables and enables benchmarking of different models on all datasets.

Observed and predicted variable values are classified into 'low', 'high', or 'normal' categories based on whether the value falls below the minimum reference interval, above the maximum reference interval, or within the reference interval, respectively.
Complementary classification labels 'not low', 'not high', and 'not normal' are assigned to observed and predicted variable values to define the specific classification task settings for evaluation.

For the NSCLC classification evaluation, the reference range parameters [v_min, v_max] were set to [14, 18] g/dL for male hemoglobin, [12, 16] g/dL for female hemoglobin, [4.5, 11.0] 10^9/L for leukocytes, [20, 40] % for leukocytes/lymphocytes, [1.0, 4.0] 10^9/L for lymphocytes, [1.8, 7.5] 10^9/L for neutrophils, and [122, 222] U/L for lactate dehydrogenase.
The model's ability to detect a significant drop in hemoglobin was evaluated by calculating AUC_low with the parameter v_min set to 7.5 g/dL.
For trend detection of all NSCLC variables, the time interval was set to 3 weeks and the parameter s was set to 21 days.
The Flatiron Health data are not publicly available, and requests for data sharing to replicate results must be submitted to PublicationsDataAccess@flatiron.com.

The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) dataset is available online at https://physionet.org/content/mimiciv, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset is available online at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data-samples/adni-data/.

The MIMIC-IV dataset is available online at https://physionet.org/content/mimiciv, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset is available online upon request under https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data-samples/adni-data/.
The code for the study is available at https://github.com/MendenLab/DT-GPT, including all package and Python versions and license information.
Specific parameters used to generate and analyze the datasets are detailed in the repository's README file and relevant configuration files.
Supplementary material for the article is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-025-02004-3. Requests for materials should be addressed to Fabian Schmich or Michael P. Menden.

The reported p-value of 0.09 is uninterpretable for replication without the corresponding effect size and 95% confidence interval, as these metrics are required to distinguish a true null effect from low statistical power.

The absence of raw logs prevents the calculation of test-retest reliability for the rationales, creating a gap that blocks the statistical distinction between a stable pattern-matching artifact and genuine logical variation.

The validation subset used only four clinicians and failed to report Cohen’s Kappa or intraclass correlation coefficients, making the confidence intervals around agreement metrics too wide to distinguish high reliability from chance alignment during replication.

The digital twin study excluded over 2,000 responses without documenting the preprocessing pipeline, creating a fatal gap that prevents independent verification of the claim that leukocyte count drives the trajectory.

The EHR-based study failed to specify the imputation strategy or protocol for handling missing lab values and rare events, making it impossible to distinguish whether the reliance on leukocyte count is a genuine clinical signal or an artifact of incomplete record processing.

The RAG retrieval similarity threshold is an unreported hyperparameter that was not tuned against a held-out validation set, rendering the reported 95% confidence intervals unreliable and preventing the reproduction of the retrieval noise control.

The validation dataset is underpowered and lacks multiple-comparison correction, relying on only four clinicians whose inter-rater reliability estimates are too noisy to support valid conclusions or independent verification of the model's safety.

Exact parameters for calculating valid effect sizes or confidence intervals are unavailable because the dependent and independent variables are derived from the same proprietary LLM source, rendering the reported accuracy metrics meaningless for replication.
Independent verification of the effect size is blocked because the unedited raw responses and the full input-output matrix are missing, preventing recalculation of the statistical results.

The statistical model is non-identifiable because the ground truth was generated by the same machine being evaluated, rendering any calculated confidence intervals invalid regardless of data availability.

Validation of reported significance differences is impossible because the raw logits and uncorrected p-values for multiple comparisons are not provided, limiting verification to descriptive statistics of inter-rater agreement with n = 4 clinicians.

Reproduction of the specific interpretability results is blocked by the missing API versions, exact prompt templates, and code for logical error quantification, even though the general workflow using hosted Claude models is reproducible.
The reported confidence intervals are unreliable because the similarity threshold was not tuned against a held-out validation set, inflating effect sizes and leaving the hyperparameters unvalidated.
A fair comparison requires a fixed dataset adjudicated by a blinded panel of experienced clinicians to establish a gold standard completely decoupled from the LLM's generation process.

The methods section fails to specify whether the four clinicians were blinded to the model outputs or the source of the ground truth, a critical missing parameter that prevents replication of a fair, decoupled evaluation.

The reported 81.5% agreement rate is statistically meaningless for a patient because the confidence intervals are inflated by the circular ground truth and lack of multiple-comparison correction, providing no reliable estimate of the error rate in actual clinical use.

The self-referential evaluation loop fails to establish any independent standard of correctness, meaning the claim that the tool supports 'triage and referral' is not supported by any verifiable baseline and remains an unproven heuristic rather than a reliable diagnostic aid.

Reproduction of the diagnostic accuracy claims is blocked because the 'clinically related' scoring criteria are subjective and lack a fixed gold standard, making it impossible to verify if the model's imprecise matches constitute genuine accuracy or merely plausible text generation.

A critical gap for replication is the absence of a standardized protocol that explicitly verifies no overlap between the held-out dataset and pre-training corpora, which prevents independent verification of the models' performance on truly unseen data.

The lack of raw inference logs and specific seed values makes it impossible to reproduce the observed consistency, as the current evidence does not isolate the model's logic from fragile implementation details or specific random seeds.

documents: The finding that GPT-4 can mimic clinical reasoning without sacrificing diagnostic accuracy is limited to the specific diagnostic reasoning prompting methods developed in this study and does not guarantee that the model's internal decision-making process is truly interpretable or distinct from uninterpretable methods.

The claim that diagnostic reasoning prompts mitigate the 'black box' limitations of large language models exceeds the evidence, as the study only demonstrates that the model can generate an interpretable rationale, which does not necessarily ensure the response is likely correct or safe for patient care.

The assertion that large language models can be integrated into clinical care based on their performance on multiple-choice questions or free-response clinical questions is an alternative explanation for their apparent competence that does not account for the lack of understanding of their actual clinical reasoning capabilities.

The exclusion of 10 NEJM Case Records from the GPT-4 evaluation because they lacked a definitive final diagnosis or exceeded the GPT-4 API's maximum context length introduces a selection bias that may limit the generalizability of the performance results to complex or ambiguous clinical scenarios.

The use of a small training set of 95 questions for iterative prompt development risks overfitting the prompts to specific question patterns, potentially inflating performance metrics on the 518-question test set and failing to capture the full range of clinical reasoning challenges.

The reliance on few-shot learning with only two example questions per prompt strategy may not adequately constrain the model's reasoning, leaving the performance of the clinical reasoning prompts vulnerable to the specific selection of those examples and potentially masking weaknesses in broader diagnostic application.

The study's evaluation of LLM diagnostic reasoning is limited to USMLE questions that assess diagnosis, excluding Step 1 questions focused on factual memorization, which means the findings may not generalize to clinical tasks requiring recall of specific medical facts rather than reasoning.

The performance assessment of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 relies on a test set of only 518 questions, which may be insufficient to robustly characterize the models' capabilities or detect subtle differences between prompting strategies across the full spectrum of clinical diagnostic scenarios.

The hypothesis that GPT models will perform superiorly with diagnostic reasoning prompts compared to traditional Chain-of-thought prompting is an unverified claim that depends on the specific implementation of prompts modeled after clinical cognitive processes, and does not account for potential confounds such as the models' pre-existing training data containing similar clinical reasoning patterns.

The assertion that newer LLMs like GPT-4 show promise in diagnosing challenging clinical cases is based on free-response evaluations, but the extent of this promise is constrained by the sensitivity of LLM outputs to prompt engineering, meaning performance may not hold if the specific instructional prompts are altered or if the questions are posed differently.

The finding that GPT-3.5's intuitive reasoning outperformed traditional Chain-of-Thought prompting is not statistically significant (p=0.4), and the confidence interval includes zero, indicating the observed 1.7% improvement may be due to random variation rather than a true effect.

The evaluation of GPT-4 on the MedQA test set is limited by a reduced sample size of 498 questions because the GPT-4 API generated errors for 20 questions, which may introduce selection bias or reduce the statistical power of the accuracy comparisons.

The comparison between GPT-4's traditional Chain-of-Thought and differential diagnosis prompting on the NEJM challenge case set is not statistically significant (p=0.09), with a confidence interval that spans both positive and negative values, suggesting the 4.2% difference in accuracy may not be reliable.

The finding that clinical reasoning rationales provide insight into LLM trustworthiness is limited because they do not offer an absolute guarantee of accuracy, meaning a logical rationale does not definitively validate the correctness of the model's final diagnostic answer.

The Bayesian inference prompt demonstrated a significant weakness by assigning arbitrary and unsupported probability values to blastomycosis, leading to a diagnosis that contradicted the specific evidence of a dimorphic fungus with septate hyphae which is characteristic of histoplasmosis.

The traditional chain-of-thought prompt exhibited a factual inaccuracy by diagnosing Valley Fever (coccidioidomycosis) despite the patient's recent hiking history in Mississippi, a region not typically associated with that specific pathogen, indicating a failure to integrate geographic epidemiological data correctly.

The finding that diagnostic reasoning prompts do not increase GPT-4 accuracy is confounded by the possibility that GPT-4 has already reached maximal diagnostic accuracy with the provided vignette information, making it impossible to detect performance differences between prompting strategies.

The conclusion that GPT-4 cannot apply clinical reasoning like a human provider may be invalid if GPT-4 is merely explaining its diagnostic evaluation post-hoc in the desired format rather than strictly utilizing the prompted diagnostic reasoning strategy.

The claim that GPT-4's reasoning mechanisms are inherently different from human providers and therefore do not benefit from diagnostic strategies is an alternative explanation that exceeds the direct evidence, as the study does not isolate the internal mechanism from the output format.

The interpretability of GPT-4's clinical reasoning rationale is limited by the fact that the logical and factual accuracy of the generated explanation does not absolutely guarantee the correctness of the final diagnostic answer.

The mitigation of 'black box' limitations through aligned model outputs is conditional on physicians recognizing that language models like GPT-4 remain at risk of unpredictable reasoning hallucinations, which undermines the reliability of the rationale.

The study's findings are limited to GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models, US-centric question sets, and the English language, meaning the results cannot be generalized to other available models, especially those fine-tuned on clinical reasoning texts, nor to non-English languages or non-US-centric contexts.

Although the prompt engineering process surveyed a wide range of styles, the investigation could not test all possible diagnostic reasoning chain-of-thought prompts, leaving unexplored variations that might alter the observed performance.

The authors explicitly state that clinical reasoning rationales provide insight but do not offer an absolute guarantee regarding the trustworthiness of LLM responses, indicating that the interpretability method has inherent limitations in predictive certainty.

The evaluation of language model responses relied on a small panel of only four physicians (three internal medicine attendings and one resident), which limits the generalizability of the grading and introduces potential evaluator bias despite the use of a third-party tie-breaker.

The finding that single-strategy prompts outperform combined strategies is confounded by the fact that GPT-4 responses did not use Demonstrate-Search-Predict or self-consistency, whereas GPT-3.5 did, making it impossible to isolate the effect of prompt strategy from the effect of model version and available inference techniques.

The Bayesian inference example provided for GPT-4 relies on arbitrary, unverified probability estimates (e.g., assuming a 10% prior probability for Histoplasmosis based on travel history) that exceed the evidence provided in the clinical vignette, demonstrating a limitation in the model's ability to ground probabilistic reasoning in objective data.

The evaluation of GPT-4 differential diagnosis rationales for logic and medical accuracy relied on only two internal medicine attending physicians, limiting the generalizability and objectivity of the clinical validity assessment.

The statistical significance threshold was adjusted to an alpha of 0.0125 via Bonferroni Correction for multiple hypotheses, which may obscure smaller but potentially clinically relevant effects that would be significant under a standard alpha of 0.05.

For GPT-3.5, the differential diagnosis prompt resulted in a statistically significant decrease in accuracy compared to traditional chain-of-thought, suggesting that this specific clinical reasoning strategy may degrade performance in less capable models.

For GPT-4, none of the clinical reasoning prompts, including differential diagnosis and Bayesian inference, demonstrated a statistically significant improvement over traditional chain-of-thought, indicating that these strategies do not reliably enhance performance in this model.

The authors declare no competing interests, but J.H.C. received research funding from Google Inc. and multiple NIH grants, which introduces a potential conflict of interest that could influence the interpretation of the large language model performance claims.

The study relies on the GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 APIs provided by OpenAI, meaning the findings are limited to the specific versions and configurations of these models at the time of access and may not generalize to other large language models or future updates.

The differential diagnosis prompting strategy showed a 4.2% lower correct response rate than traditional chain-of-thought prompting for GPT-4 on the NEJM challenge set, but this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.09), suggesting the advantage of the traditional method is not robustly established in this specific comparison.

The evaluation of LLM diagnostic reasoning relied on reviewers who were blinded to the index question and gold standard answer, a condition that may limit the ability to detect subtle inaccuracies or false logic that would be apparent with full clinical context.

The reported p-value cannot be interpreted as evidence against the null hypothesis without knowing if multiple comparisons were adjusted, as an uncorrected alpha inflates the Type I error rate regardless of the sample size or observed variance.

Reproducibility of the logical error quantification is currently impossible because the specific API version, exact prompt templates, and software configuration are missing, leaving open the alternative explanation that the results are not robust to minor changes in the input environment.

The study's evaluation of large language models is limited to a curated dataset of 2000 medical cases derived from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care database, which may not represent the full diversity of real-world clinical presentations or patient populations.

The claim that large language models offer a promising approach to improving patient outcomes is speculative, as the study only demonstrates that these models are capable of providing insights into diagnoses and specialists without establishing a causal link to improved clinical results.

The potential of large language models to mitigate under-triage and over-triage in emergency departments remains an emerging area of research, as their application in real-world, open-ended clinical scenarios has not yet been validated against structured environments like medical licensing exams.

While large language models show promise in structured settings, their capability to improve patient management and triage in dynamic, unstructured clinical environments is limited by the fact that this application remains an area of active research and development rather than a proven solution.

The study's reliance on a dataset of 2000 real-world cases from the MIMIC-IV database limits the generalizability of the findings regarding the performance of Claude family LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation workflows.
