documents: The study utilized a modified MedQA USMLE dataset consisting of 95 questions in a training set for prompt development and 518 questions in a test set for evaluation.

The study used a training set of 95 questions for iterative prompt development and a test set of 518 questions for evaluation. GPT-4 performance was evaluated on 310 cases from the New England Journal of Medicine Case Records series, with 10 cases excluded due to the absence of a definitive final diagnosis or exceeding the GPT-4 API maximum context length.

The evaluation compared traditional Chain-of-Thought prompting to the highest performing clinical reasoning Chain-of-Thought prompt (differential diagnosis reasoning) on the modified MedQA dataset. One traditional Chain-of-Thought prompt and four clinical reasoning prompts (differential diagnosis, analytical, Bayesian, and intuitive reasoning) were developed, with each prompt including two example questions and rationales employing the target reasoning strategy in a few-shot learning technique.
The inter-rater agreement for the GPT-4 NEJM evaluation was 97% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.93.
GPT-3.5 performance was significantly worse with differential diagnosis and analytical CoT prompts compared to traditional and intuitive reasoning CoT prompts.
Bayesian inference CoT demonstrated worse performance than traditional CoT for GPT-3.5, but the decrease in performance did not meet the study's significance threshold.
GPT-4 demonstrated similar performance between traditional and diagnostic reasoning CoT prompts, indicating that diagnostic reasoning does not increase GPT-4 accuracy.

The study's evaluation was limited to GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models, US-centric question sets, and the English language, which restricts generalization to other models, non-English languages, and non-US-centric question sets.
The study could not test all possible diagnostic reasoning chain-of-thought prompts, representing a limitation in the comprehensiveness of the prompt engineering process.

In the evaluation of 100 GPT-4 diagnostic reasoning rationales, 65% of incorrect answers contained false logic statements in their rationale, with an average of 0.82 inaccuracies per rationale. In contrast, only 18% of correct answers contained false logic statements, with an average of 0.11 inaccuracies per question.

In a Bayesian Inference Chain-of-Thought example for a patient with a dimorphic fungus, the prior probability of blastomycosis was 1%, increasing to 5% with recent travel, 30% with laboratory and urinalysis results, and 60% with the presence of a dimorphic fungus on bronchoalveolar lavage.
A scratching murmur increases the probability of a specific condition to 10%, and in the setting of a recent myocardial infarction, the posterior probability of myocardial infarction is 55%.

GPT-3.5 achieved 46% accuracy with traditional CoT prompting compared to 31% with zero-shot non-CoT prompting, and 48% with intuitive reasoning (difference of +1.7%, CI -2.5% to +5.9%, p=0.4). GPT-3.5 performance was significantly worse with analytic reasoning (40%, difference of -6%, CI -11% to -1.5%, p=0.001) and differential diagnosis formation (38%, difference of -8.9%, CI -14% to -3.4%, p<0.001), while Bayesian inference performance was 42% (difference of -4.4%, CI -9.1% to +0.2%, p=0.02).
Inter-rater agreement for the MedQA GPT-3.5 evaluation was 97% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.93.
The GPT-4 API generated an error for 20 questions of the test set, reducing the GPT-4 test set size to 498.

GPT-4 achieved 76% accuracy with traditional CoT, 77% with intuitive reasoning (difference of +0.8%, CI -3.6% to +5.2%, p=0.73), 78% with differential diagnosis (difference of +2.2%, CI -2.3% to +6.7%, p=0.24), 78% with analytic reasoning (difference of +1.6%, CI -2.4% to +5.6%, p=0.35), and 72% with Bayesian Inference (difference of -3.4%, CI -9.1% to +1.2%, p=0.07).
Inter-rater agreement for the GPT-4 MedQA evaluation was 99% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.98.
On the NEJM challenge case set, GPT-4 achieved 38% accuracy with traditional CoT compared to 34% with differential diagnosis CoT (difference of -4.2%, 95% CI -11.4% to +2.1%, p=0.09).

Language model responses were evaluated by physician authors AN, ER, RG, and TS, comprising three internal medicine attending physicians and one internal medicine resident, with each question evaluated by two blinded physicians and a third evaluator determining the final grade in cases of disagreement.

The evaluation utilized the OpenAI Davinci-003 model via an OpenAI API for GPT-3.5 responses and the GPT-4 model via an OpenAI API for GPT-4 responses, with GPT-3.5 prompting performed using the Demonstrate-Search-Predict (DSP) method.

Self-consistency was applied to all GPT-3.5 Chain-of-Thought prompts, whereas GPT-4 responses did not use DSP or self-consistency because those features were not available for GPT-4 at the time of submission.

GPT-4 achieved 38% correct responses with chain-of-thought prompting and 34% with differential diagnosis prompting on the NEJM challenge question set, a difference of -4.2% (95% CI: -11.4%, +2.1%) with a p-value of 0.09.

Statistical significance and confidence intervals were calculated against traditional Chain of Thought using McNemar's test for paired proportions, two-tailed, with a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of 0.0125 to account for four prompts per model. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen's Kappa Statistic, and statistical analysis was performed in R with the epibasix library.
The first 100 GPT-4 differential diagnosis rationales were evaluated for appropriate logic and medical accuracy by physician authors RG and TS, who are both internal medicine attending physicians.

For GPT-3.5 on the MEDQA question set, the Intuitive reasoning prompt achieved 48% correct responses (difference 1.7%, 95% CI -2.5% to 5.9%, p=0.4) and the Analytic reasoning prompt achieved 40% correct responses (difference -6.0%, 95% CI -11% to -1.5%, p=0.001) compared to the 46% baseline for traditional Chain of Thought. The Differential diagnosis prompt achieved 38% correct responses (difference -8.9%, 95% CI -14% to -3.4%, p<0.001) and the Bayesian inference prompt achieved 42% correct responses (difference -4.4%, 95% CI -9.1% to 0.2%, p=0.02) compared to the traditional Chain of Thought baseline.

The study benchmarked multiple large language model versions and a retrieval-augmented generation workflow on a curated dataset of 2000 medical cases derived from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care database.
Trauma systems set goals to minimize under-triage at ≤ 5% and accept a higher rate of over-triage at ≤ 35% to reduce mortality caused by under-triage.
A review of field triage performance showed 14% to 34% under-triaged cases across all ages, while over-triage rates were shown to be between 12% and 31%.
The study utilized a knowledge base of 30 million PubMed abstracts to improve output with domain-specific context.

The study benchmarked multiple LLM workflows, including multiple versions of the Claude family and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agentic workflow, using a dataset of 2000 real-world cases from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) database.
The curated MIMIC-IV ED dataset consists of 2000 medical cases extracted from fully de-identified electronic health records and MIMIC-IV Notes.
The RAG-assisted LLM utilizes a knowledge base of 30 million PubMed abstracts to provide domain-specific context for Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

The study evaluated LLM triage prediction using two metrics: exact match accuracy, where the predicted Emergency Severity Index (ESI) level equaled the actual value, and triage range accuracy, where predictions were correct if they were exactly or one ESI level higher than the actual level, with the constraint that ESI level 1 had to be predicted as 1.
No model achieved high accuracy in predicting the most severe triage levels, but none of the models confused the most critical cases with the least serious ones.
When a model misclassified the triage level, the error was usually within the range of one level more severe.
A slight decline in triage range accuracy was noted across most cases, except for Claude 3 Haiku, which struggled strongly to process the additional information from the initial vitals effectively.

In the evaluation checking if at least one of the top three predicted specialties is correct, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved the highest performance, while overall performance differences remained small across all models.
The improvement between general user and clinician user models was most evident in the Claude 3.5 Sonnet model, with only minimal improvements seen in the RAG-assisted LLM and Claude 3 Haiku.
Claude 3 Sonnet experienced a negative impact on specialty prediction performance when provided with additional information about the initial vitals.

Table 2 reports performance improvements for each model from general user to clinical user settings, with RAG-Assisted LLM showing an average improvement of 0.34 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet showing an average improvement of 0.51.

For diagnosis evaluation, the RAG-Assisted LLM achieved an exact match score of 0.34 and an at-least-one score of 0.85, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an exact match score of 0.04 and an at-least-one score of 0.10.
Four clinicians reviewed a subset of the data to validate the use of Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a judge for comparing predicted diagnoses to ground truth diagnoses.
Across all clinicians, 81.5% of LLM-generated specialty predictions were rated as Correct, with an overall error rate of 2.63% and a combined acceptability rate of 97.03%.
Clinician 2 exhibited a higher error rate of 9.15% compared to the average error rate of 0.68% for the other clinicians.
Four clinicians participated in the inter-rater agreement evaluation, where each pair of clinicians assessed the same subset to ensure independent evaluations.

In the Union scenario, where an LLM evaluation was considered correct if at least one of two clinicians agreed, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an accuracy of 95.62% and the RAG-assisted LLM achieved an accuracy of 94.91%.

In the Intersection scenario, where an LLM evaluation was considered correct only if both clinicians agreed, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an accuracy of 70.74% and the RAG-assisted LLM achieved an accuracy of 69.86%.
The average inter-model agreement for the category 'Between General and Clinical User' was 86.04%, with individual model scores ranging from 83.54% for Claude 3 Haiku to 89.74% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

The average inter-model agreement for the category 'To RAG-Assisted LLM' was 78.29%, with agreement values of 83.88% from Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 76.64% from Claude 3 Sonnet, and 74.34% from Claude 3 Haiku.

The average inter-model agreement for the category 'To Claude 3.5 Sonnet' was 78.14%, with agreement values of 83.88% from RAG-Assisted LLM, 77.19% from Claude 3 Sonnet, and 73.35% from Claude 3 Haiku.

The average inter-model agreement for the category 'To Claude 3 Haiku' was 74.44%, with agreement values of 74.34% from RAG-Assisted LLM, 73.35% from Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and 75.65% from Claude 3 Sonnet.
Clinician 1 evaluated the LLM-generated specialties with 93.77% accuracy, 6.23% acceptability, 100% combined accuracy and acceptability, and a 0% error rate.
The average evaluation across all clinicians for LLM-generated specialties was 81.5% accuracy, 15.53% acceptability, 97.03% combined accuracy and acceptability, and a 2.63% error rate.

In a benchmark of 2000 real-world medical cases from the MIMIC-IV-ED dataset, the average inter-rater union accuracy was 95.62% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 94.91% for the RAG-assisted LLM, while the average inter-rater intersection accuracy was 70.74% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 69.86% for the RAG-assisted LLM.

The individual inter-rater accuracy for Claude 3.5 Sonnet ranged from 76.51% for Clinician 3 to 90.43% for Clinician 1, and for the RAG-assisted LLM, it ranged from 77.78% for Clinician 3 to 90.11% for Clinician 1.

The inter-rater intersection accuracy for the pair of Clinicians 1 and 2 was 75.44% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 73.84% for the RAG-assisted LLM, whereas for the pair of Clinicians 3 and 4, it was 66.03% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 65.87% for the RAG-assisted LLM.

The RAG-assisted LLM demonstrated a significant performance improvement in triage level and diagnosis tasks when using the clinical user setting with additional patient vitals data, whereas the base model Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed improvements in triage level and specialty tasks but gained less from vital signs in the diagnosis task.

The RAG-assisted LLM achieved strong exact accuracy on triage level data with vital signs information, but this external reference capability did not improve the model's range accuracy for predicting more severe versus less severe conditions.
The study utilized the MIMIC-IV ED dataset and MIMIC-IV Notes dataset to process data for a model predicting specialty, triage level, and diagnosis in an emergency department setting.
The preprocessing pipeline filtered records to retain only those with sequence number (seq_num) equal to 1 to ensure the uniqueness of emergency department stays and excluded patients that had died.

The unstructured clinical notes preprocessing step selected only cases with History of Present Illness (HPI) string lengths between 50 and 2000 characters and removed entries that mentioned "ED" or "ER".
The evaluation used only primary diagnoses and discarded cases that had more than 15 primary diagnoses, noting that most cases had up to 3 diagnoses.
The RAG system's knowledge base consists of 30 million PubMed abstracts converted into embedding vectors and stored in a high-dimensional vector database.
The RAG system's workflow utilizes 30 million PubMed abstracts converted into embedding vectors for semantic similarity comparison.

The temperature parameter was set to zero during experiments, resulting in identical results across runs with no variations, which justified running the LLM predictions only once for the final evaluation.

The evaluation utilized the MIMIC-IV-ED 2.2 and MIMIC-IV-Note datasets from Physionet, with data tables merged and clinical notes processed to extract history of present illness and primary diagnoses.

The triage level evaluation framework uses the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) with five levels, and the second assessment framework allows model predictions to be one level lower than the ground truth for real values of 2 through 5, while requiring an exact match for a real value of 1.

The specialty evaluation framework assesses Large Language Models by generating the top three specialty recommendations for general users based on symptom descriptions and basic patient information, and for clinical users based on augmented input including initial vital signs.
The evaluation methodology involved four clinicians who compared predicted diagnoses to ground truth diagnoses on a subset of the dataset.

The first evaluation method for specialty prediction calculated a per-patient score by dividing the count of correctly predicted specialties by the length of the shorter list (either the ground truth or the prediction list), then summed these points and divided by the total number of patients to calculate overall accuracy.
The second evaluation framework for specialty prediction defined a patient's prediction as successful if at least one of the model's predicted specialties appeared in the ground truth list.

The study used Claude 3.5 Sonnet to predict the most likely specialist for each diagnosis to establish ground truth, as the MIMIC-IV-ED and MIMIC-IV-Notes datasets lack exact information on the medical specialist each patient visited.

The evaluation framework predicted a top three list of specialists for each case to address the complexity of patients presenting with multiple simultaneous medical conditions, rather than predicting a single specialist.

The diagnosis evaluation framework predicted a top three list of diagnoses for each case and confirmed that all evaluation cases had a hospital stay duration of less than one day to minimize the inclusion of diagnoses arising later during hospitalization.

The study selected a subset of 400 cases out of 2000 total cases, assigning 200 cases to each of four clinicians, with Clinicians 1 and 2 reviewing the same subset and Clinicians 3 and 4 reviewing a different subset to enable independent evaluations.
A subset of the dataset was validated by four clinicians to assess the reliability and interpretability of the LLM evaluation tool.

The reader study involved four clinicians from different institutions: one from Policlinico Gemelli in Rome, Italy, one from the Radiology Department at Klinikum rechts der Isar in Munich, Germany, and two from the University of Chicago in the United States.

The LLM judge evaluated predicted diagnoses by determining if the three predicted diagnoses matched the true list of diagnoses for each patient via semantic equivalence or by falling under a broader related category. The LLM judge returned "True" if a match or broader relation existed, and "False" otherwise.

Prior research indicates that LLMs can perform human-like evaluations in tasks such as text summarization and quality assessments with results aligning closely to human judgments, supporting the use of LLMs for diagnostic comparison evaluation.
The study evaluated the agreement between eight model variants, consisting of the RAG-assisted model and the three Claude language models with general user and clinical user settings.
Intra-model agreement was calculated separately for triage level predictions and specialty predictions, with results presented in a symmetrical matrix that excluded self-comparisons.

The study lacks specified temperature and top-k sampling parameters for inference on the modified MedQA and NEJM datasets, meaning observed reliability may reflect stochastic variance rather than the effect of diagnostic reasoning prompts.
Reproducibility is blocked by missing raw data, analysis code, and software versions, specifically requiring exact parameter settings and randomization seed values to verify the reported numbers.

Verification of variance is impeded by the absence of the specific API version, exact prompt templates, and the code for logical error quantification, despite the availability of full LLM response and rationale results in the supplementary materials.

The inability to isolate the source of interpretability arises because the methods section leaves unspecified whether the self-consistency sampling for GPT-3.5 used a fixed number of generations or a dynamic stopping rule, preventing the separation of Bayesian logic effects from the averaging effect of the sampling.

DT-GPT reduced the scaled mean absolute error by 3.4% on the non-small cell lung cancer dataset, 1.3% on the intensive care unit dataset, and 1.8% on the Alzheimer's disease dataset compared to state-of-the-art machine learning models.
DT-GPT overcomes real-world data challenges including missingness, noise, and limited sample sizes without requiring data imputation or normalization.

The DT-GPT model was evaluated on an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) dataset derived from MIMIC-IV containing 35,131 patients, a non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) dataset from the Flatiron Health EHR-derived database containing 16,496 patients, and an Alzheimer's Disease dataset from ADNI containing 1,140 patients.
On the NSCLC dataset, DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.55 ± 0.04, outperforming LightGBM (0.57 ± 0.05) by a relative improvement of 3.4%.
On the ICU dataset, DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.59 ± 0.03, outperforming LightGBM (0.60 ± 0.03) by a relative improvement of 1.3%.
On the Alzheimer's disease dataset, DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.47 ± 0.03, outperforming Temporal Fusion Transformer (0.48 ± 0.02) by a relative improvement of 1.8%.
DT-GPT demonstrated statistical significance over the second-best performing model on the NSCLC dataset with a p-value < 9.6162 × 10^-17 and on the ICU dataset with a p-value < 0.00043.
DT-GPT outperformed Bio-Mistral by 47.9%, 29.1%, and 61.1% on the NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's disease datasets, respectively.
DT-GPT outperformed the Qwen3-32B model by 22.9%, 19.9%, and 21.1% on the NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's disease datasets, respectively.

DT-GPT achieved the lowest scaled mean absolute error (MAE) across all 12 benchmark variables in the non-small cell lung cancer, intensive care unit, and Alzheimer's disease datasets, with specific MAE values ranging from 0.417 to 0.701 for DT-GPT compared to baselines like LightGBM (0.425 to 0.734) and Linear Regression (0.449 to 0.782). All model comparisons were performed on unseen patients.

The study compared DT-GPT against 14 multi-step, multivariate baselines, including Linear Regression, LightGBM, Temporal Fusion Transformer, Temporal Convolutional Network, Recurrent Neural Network, Long Short-Term Memory, Transformer, and Time-series Dense Encoder, as well as channel-independent models PatchTST, Time-LLM, and LLMTime.

The evaluation included general and biomedical large language models Qwen3-32B (32 billion parameters) and BioMistral-7B (7 billion parameters), with DT-GPT identified as a fine-tuned 7-billion-parameter model based on BioMistral.

In the non-small cell lung cancer dataset, the forecasting task involved predicting six laboratory values weekly for up to 13 weeks post-therapy initiation, while the intensive care unit task forecasted respiratory rate, magnesium, and oxygen saturation for the next 24 hours based on the previous 24-hour history.

For the Alzheimer's disease dataset, the model forecasted Mini Mental State Examination, Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes, and Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale cognitive scores over the next 24 months at 6-month intervals using baseline measurements.
DT-GPT outperformed Bio-Mistral by 47.9%, 29.1%, and 61.1%, and outperformed Qwen3-32B by 22.9%, 19.9%, and 21.1% on NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's disease datasets, respectively.
DT-GPT achieved a ROC AUC of 0.506 for forecasting critically low hemoglobin levels (<7.5 g/dL), a result attributed to the low prevalence of 1.2% for this condition.
The prediction of high leukocyte counts (>11.0 x 10^9/L) by DT-GPT yielded a ROC AUC of 0.578, which was lower than the copy-forward baseline ROC AUC of 0.616.
DT-GPT demonstrated a ROC AUC of 0.793 for detecting mild anemia (hemoglobin below reference) and a ROC AUC of 0.793 for detecting elevated lactate dehydrogenase (>222 U/L).
DT-GPT captured three-week trends in hemoglobin with ROC AUCs of 0.704 for increasing trends and 0.638 for decreasing trends.
DT-GPT achieved ROC AUCs ranging from 0.65 to 0.68 for capturing rising leukocytes, lymphocytes, and neutrophils suggestive of inflammation.

The correlations between variables forecasted by DT-GPT aligned with test dataset correlations with an R^2 of 0.98 on the NSCLC dataset and 0.99 on the ICU dataset, compared to LightGBM R^2 values of 0.97 and 0.99, respectively.
For the Alzheimer's disease dataset, both DT-GPT and the TFT model achieved an R^2 of 0.99 for inter-variable relationship preservation.

DT-GPT performance was competitive with baselines after training on data corresponding to 5,000 patients and improved with increasing patient numbers in the training dataset. DT-GPT performance degradation occurred only after more than 20% of input was randomly masked, which was in addition to the 94.4% initial missingness of the NSCLC dataset.
DT-GPT performance significantly degraded only after 25 misspellings per patient sample were introduced. Explanatory variables were extracted from 25,575 out of 27,730 chatbot responses.
The last recorded ECOG value in a patient's medical history was predictive of future hemoglobin levels, with lower ECOG values correlating with higher hemoglobin levels over time.
DT-GPT forecasted 69 non-target clinical variables, extracting 81,004 trajectories from 81,918 forecasting results.
The benchmarking experiment involved 69 LightGBM models, each trained on data from over 13,000 patients for individual target variables, compared against a single zero-shot DT-GPT model.
Zero-shot DT-GPT outperformed LightGBM on 13 out of 69 non-target variables.

Segmented neutrophils, band form neutrophils, and neutrophils by automated count have LOINC codes 30451-9, 26507-4, and 751-8, respectively, which are functionally related to the target variable neutrophils (LOINC 26499-4).

DT-GPT demonstrated equal or superior performance compared to the LightGBM baseline for 11 of 13 non-target variables, where these 11 variables exhibited a strong Spearman correlation coefficient (|ρ| > 0.7) with at least one fine-tuned target variable.
The NSCLC dataset utilized for robustness testing had a baseline missingness rate of 94.4%.
For the Alzheimer's disease dataset, both DT-GPT and the second-best model TFT achieved an R² of 0.99.
The final DT-GPT prediction was derived by averaging 30 generated trajectories.

Selecting individual trajectories with the lowest scaled MAE and recalculating the hypothetical scaled MAE on the NSCLC dataset achieved a 26% improvement in error to 0.40 ± 0.02 without further model training.
The distribution of scaled MAE for neutrophils across all patients was right-skewed, indicating that high errors originated from a small number of patients with likely uncommon trajectories.
DT-GPT exhibited the lowest median Kolmogorov-Smirnov score among all models when comparing predicted and true distributions across all target variables in the NSCLC cohort.

Recent baselines including TiDE, TCN, and TFT struggled with distribution modeling, while LLMTime had the second lowest mean Kolmogorov-Smirnov score and LightGBM was the best performing baseline with respect to scaled MAE.
The NSCLC dataset had a baseline missingness rate of 94.4%.
LightGBM achieved the lowest scaled MAE after DT-GPT.
The single DT-GPT model outperforms 69 separate LightGBM models on 13 out of 69 non-target variables.
Zero-shot DT-GPT outperforms a supervised, fully-trained machine learning model on a subset of clinical variables.
The underlying BioMistral 7B model was trained on a vast amount of biomedical databases and publications.
DT-GPT demonstrates strong performance on standard metrics, specifically Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
DT-GPT performance declines for specific acute events, such as severe hemoglobin drops or high leukocyte counts, which are characterized as low-prevalence, high-variance outcomes.
The current constraint on the number of forecasted variables is due to the limited sequence length of both input and output of the Large Language Models (LLMs) used in fine-tuning.
Advances in extending the context length will enable modeling of additional patient variables by using larger, more advanced models such as Qwen3-32B as the base model.

DT-GPT was trained and evaluated for forecasting patients' laboratory values across three independent datasets: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), intensive care unit (ICU), and Alzheimer's disease patients.
The US-based NSCLC dataset originated from approximately 280 cancer clinics, representing approximately 800 sites of care.

The study included 16,496 patients diagnosed with NSCLC from 01 January 1991 to 06 July 2023, sourced from approximately 280 cancer clinics (~800 sites of care). The dataset comprised 773,607 patient-days across 320 variables, focusing on the 50 most common diagnoses and 80 most common laboratory measurements.
The ICU analysis utilized the MIMIC-IV dataset, resulting in 300 input variables across 1,686,288 time points from 35,131 patients.

The missing data study randomly masked between 0 and 80% of data and evaluated the effect on a randomly sampled 200 patients from the test set, a sample size noted to potentially lead to higher variance in the results.

The noise study applied a misspelling algorithm that randomly performs perturbation, insertion, deletion, or replacement operations using all ASCII letters and digits on the entire input text, where one operation is defined as one misspelling.
The evaluation of the effects of real-world data missingness and noise was performed on a randomly sampled 200 patients from the test set.

The MIMIC-IV dataset processing pipeline yielded 300 input variables across 1,686,288 time points from 35,131 patients. The forecasting task required predicting future 24 hourly values for O2 saturation pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, and magnesium, with the selection criteria requiring at least 50% of patients to have at least one measurement for each variable.

The Alzheimer's disease dataset derived from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) included 1140 patients. The task involved predicting the 24-month trajectory of Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes (CDR-SB), and Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS11) based on baseline measurements.

The NSCLC and ICU datasets were split at the patient level into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test sets, with the ICU split performed randomly and the NSCLC split stratified by group stage, smoking status, number of observations per visit, and number of visits with drug administrations.
The Alzheimer's disease dataset was randomly split into 80% training and 20% test sets due to the small sample size, with all hyperparameters determined via a further splitting on the training set.

A two-step outlier filtering procedure was applied to all datasets, first filtering target values below or above three standard deviations, then calculating new standard deviation values on the filtered dataset and clipping target values below and above those new values.
The data for all baselines excluding DT-GPT were standardized using z-scores.

The Spearman correlation coefficient is calculated using a rank function that assigns the average rank to data points with identical values, with mean ranks for actual and predicted values defined as the average of the time-averaged ranks across all samples.
Scaled MAE is selected as the primary metric to enable comparison across all variables and benchmark different models on all datasets.

Observed variable values are labeled as "low" if below the reference minimum, "high" if above the reference maximum, and "normal" if within the reference interval, with predicted values labeled analogously to establish a classification task.

The multiclass classification performance metric AUC weighted is calculated as the weighted average of AUC_low, AUC_normal, and AUC_high, where the weights are the counts of observed variable values labeled as "low", "normal", and "high" respectively to account for class imbalance.

A predicted value v_t^(i) is classified as a 'decreasing trend' only if v_{k+1}^(i) < v_k^(i) for all time steps k within the interval [time(t)-s, time(t)], and as an 'increasing trend' only if v_{k+1}^(i) > v_k^(i) for all k in that same interval.

Trend classification performance is quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for the binary tasks 'decreasing' versus 'not decreasing' and 'increasing' versus 'not increasing', denoted as AUC_trend↓ and AUC_trend↑, with forecasted values excluded if time(t) < s to ensure a complete lookback window.
The study randomly sampled 200 patients from the test set, a choice that potentially leads to higher variance in the results.

The forecasting metrics used to quantify disparity between predicted and observed values are mean absolute error (MAE), scaled MAE, mean absolute scaled error (MASE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE), and Spearman correlation coefficient.
Scaled MAE is defined as the mean absolute error divided by the standard deviation of the clinical variable after outlier filtering.
Mean absolute scaled error (MASE) is defined as the mean absolute error divided by the average absolute difference between observed values and the baseline value.

Symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE) is defined as the sum of 200 times the ratio of the absolute difference between observed and predicted values to the sum of their absolute values, multiplied by an indicator function to avoid division by zero.

The classification evaluation was performed exclusively on NSCLC data using literature-derived reference ranges: hemoglobin [14, 18] g/dL for males and [12, 16] g/dL for females, leukocytes [4.5, 11.0] 10^9/L, leukocytes/lymphocytes [20, 40] %, lymphocytes [1.0, 4.0] 10^9/L, neutrophils [1.8, 7.5] 10^9/L, and lactate dehydrogenase [122, 222] U/L.
The model's ability to detect a significant hemoglobin drop associated with bleeding was evaluated by calculating AUC_low with a v_min threshold of 7.5.
For trend detection in NSCLC variables, the analysis used time intervals of 3 weeks and set the lookback window parameter s to 21 days.

The primary finding of a 1.7% performance difference for the intuitive reasoning prompt is statistically indistinguishable from zero because the confidence interval spans negative to positive values, which fails to demonstrate a robust, reproducible effect for model interpretability.

The claim that leukocyte count drives the trajectory in the digital twin framework is unsupported by evidence due to the undocumented exclusion of over two thousand responses, creating a gap that prevents independent verification of the model's core logic.

The model's reliance on variables like leukocyte count may be a byproduct of how incomplete records were processed rather than a genuine clinical signal, as the methods section leaves unspecified how missing lab values or rare events in the sparse, heterogeneous EHR data were handled before input into the LLM.

The reported 95% confidence interval of -2.5% to 5.9% for the 1.7% difference between the LLM and the reference standard precludes independent verification of whether this effect is stable or attributable to seed variance, particularly because the wide interval encompasses zero and the raw inference logs required to test this hypothesis were not provided.

The transition from a statistically indistinguishable 1.7% difference to a live clinical trial is unsupported by the data because the unreported RAG retrieval threshold prevents the exclusion of retrieval bias, meaning the model's outputs may be artifacts of irrelevant noise rather than genuine clinical context.

The ground truth for specialist referral was derived from Claude 3.5 Sonnet's predictions rather than verified clinical records, creating a circularity bias that measures agreement with an LLM's output rather than actual medical necessity.

Reproduction of the inter-rater analysis is blocked by the missing individual clinician ratings and raw model outputs, which are required to calculate the confidence interval on the Kappa statistic for the four-person sample.

The evaluation design fails to report the exact embedding model or similarity threshold for the RAG retrieval pipeline, preventing verification of whether the results are grounded in relevant literature or are an artifact of the retrieval process.

The observed accuracy in the specialist referral benchmark may be attributed to pattern-matching the idiosyncratic biases of the four raters rather than genuine diagnostic logic, as the system lacks evidence of real-world efficacy outside the closed, unverified generation loop.

Replication of the reasoning prompt study is blocked by missing specific RAG retrieval logs and unedited model responses, preventing verification of whether the generated 'reasoning' is derived from retrieval or generation, despite the availability of prompt templates and model versions.

The similarity threshold used in the comparison was not tuned against a held-out validation set, a methodological flaw that inflates apparent effect sizes and renders the reported confidence intervals unreliable.

The study reports an 81.5% 'correct' rate, but this metric is compromised by a self-referential loop where the clinical baseline is defined by the same model being evaluated rather than independent expertise.

The methods section fails to specify whether the four clinicians were blinded to the model outputs or the source of the ground truth, a missing parameter that invalidates the fairness of the comparison due to the entanglement of the LLM and clinical baseline in the same generation loop.

The safety claim that the LLM tool is not a replacement for care is not reproducible without a fixed benchmark and version history, as the absence of validation logs prevents verification that the model has not drifted.
